newsitem.title: USA: Stratus, Tandem both report strong earnings.
newsitem.headline: Stratus, Tandem both report strong earnings.

text.p: Stratus Computer Inc. and Tandem Computers Inc., two rival developers of fail-safe computers, both reported better-than-expected earnings Tuesday amid strong sales to the telecommunications and financial industries.
The two companies develop so-called "fault-tolerant" computers used by stock exchanges, banks, telephone companies and many others who need their systems to run 24 hours a day.

"They were both a bit better than expected," said Steve Milunovich, a Morgan Stanley analyst. "Telecommunications spending must be fairly strong because they both benefit a lot from that." Milunovich raised his rating on Stratus and said he was looking at upping his earnings estimates.

Stratus, of Marlboro, Mass., reported first quarter earnings that surpassed Wall Street estimates, with net income of $14.8 million, or 62 cents per share, compared with $10.6 million, or 45 cents a share a year earlier. According to First Call, the consensus estimate among analysts was 49 cents a share.
Revenues were up 9 percent to $155.7 million, from $142.9 million in the previous year's first quarter.
"Revenues and earnings set new first quarter records for Stratus," said Stratus Chairman Bill Foster.
"Stratus had a blow-out quarter," said John Jones, a Salomon Brothers analyst. "Revenue was a little bit better than my expectations and gross margins were better."
Stratus said it looked forward to a strong performance in the second quarter and said 1997 "will be a very good year."
Stratus said its product revenues grew at 17 percent, including 15 percent in hardware revenues and 31 percent growth in application software licensing revenues.
Sales in financial services were strong, up 38 percent, and telecommunications were up 58 percent, Stratus said.
One customer, New T&T in Hong Kong, implemented the world's first local number portability service running on a Stratus Continuum system.

Tandem Computers, based in Cupertino, Calif., also had a good quarter, reporting fiscal second quarter net income of $26 million, or 22 cents a share, compared with a loss of $49.6 million, or 42 cents a share a year ago, which included a $52 million restructuring charge.

But the stronger dollar had a negative impact of 2.9 percent on revenues, which fell to $467 million in the fiscal second quarter from $470 million a year ago. A stronger dollar makes sales in foreign currencies worth less in dollar terms.

Tandem said demand for its high-end NonStop Himalaya K2000 Server computers remained strong and that sales of the mid-range K-series server computers were up 22 percent from the year-ago period. Servers link computers in networks.
All geographical divisions reported quarterly revenues close to target, with 76 percent of its sales coming from Tandem's primary markets in telecommunications and finance.
Tandem, which has been restructuring, said its product profit margins improved 2.3 points to 58 percent of revenues.
Expenses declined year-over-year with marketing, general and administrative expenses down $12 million to $140 million.
Tandem also said it expects shipments of its new systems running Microsoft Corp.'s Windows NT software would rise significantly over the next two quarters.
Tandem said its cash position improved signficantly, both quarter over quarter, and year over year, with a corresponding decline in its debt.

"Our transformation continues according to plan," Tandem Chief Executive Officer Roel Pieper said in a statement. "It is clear that our vision and strategy are on target and have returned Tandem to growth and profitability."
Tandem also said it plans to launch a suite of NonStop Software products next month.
Tandem stock was down 12.5 cents at $12.50 and Stratus was up $1.875 at $33.25 on the New York Stock Exchange in afternoon trading.
